cards.definition: A whole number that can be positive, negative or zero, e.g. -3, 0, 7.
A whole number that divides exactly into another number with no remainder.
The result of multiplying a number by a positive integer, e.g. multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12…
A number greater than 1 that has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
A factor of a number that is also a prime number.
The largest number that is a factor of two or more given numbers.
The smallest number that is a multiple of two or more given numbers.
The result of multiplying a whole number by itself, e.g. 25 = 5 × 5.
The result of multiplying a whole number by itself twice, e.g. 27 = 3 × 3 × 3.
The small raised number showing how many times a base is multiplied by itself, e.g. 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2.
A number written as one integer divided by another, representing a part of a whole, e.g. ¾.
The top number in a fraction, representing how many parts are taken.
The bottom number in a fraction, representing the total number of equal parts.
Fractions that represent the same value, e.g. ½ and 4/8.
A fraction where the numerator is greater than the denominator, e.g. 7/4.
A number written as a whole number and a proper fraction, e.g. 1¾.
A number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100, denoted by the symbol %.
The change in a value expressed as a percentage of the original: (change ÷ original) × 100.
A decimal in which one or more digits repeat infinitely, e.g. 0.333… = ⅓.
A decimal that has a finite number of digits after the decimal point, e.g. 0.75.
Reducing a number to a given number of decimal places or significant figures to make it simpler.
The meaningful digits in a number, starting from the first non-zero digit.
The number of digits after the decimal point in a rounded value.
Finding an approximate answer by rounding values to easy numbers before calculating.
The highest value a rounded number could have been before rounding.
The lowest value a rounded number could have been before rounding.
The range of values a number could take, written as lower bound ≤ x < upper bound.
An irrational root that cannot be expressed exactly as a decimal, e.g. √2 or √5.
Rewriting a fraction so there is no surd in the denominator, e.g. 1/√3 becomes √3/3.
A way of writing very large or small numbers as A × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ A < 10.
A mathematical phrase containing numbers, variables and operations, but no equals sign, e.g. 3x + 2.
A mathematical statement that two expressions are equal, containing an equals sign, e.g. 3x + 2 = 11.
A rule written with mathematical symbols that describes a relationship between quantities.
An equation that is true for all values of the variable, shown by the ≡ symbol.
To collect like terms or reduce an expression to its simplest equivalent form.
To multiply out brackets so every term inside is multiplied by the term outside.
To write an expression as a product of its factors by taking common factors outside brackets.
Terms in an expression that have the same variable and power and can be combined.
The numerical value multiplying a variable in a term, e.g. in 5x, the coefficient is 5.
Replacing variables in an expression or formula with given numerical values.
An equation where the highest power of the variable is 1, producing a straight-line graph.
An equation where the highest power of the variable is 2, in the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Finding solutions to a quadratic by writing it as a product of two brackets and setting each to zero.
A formula used to solve any quadratic: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a.
Rewriting a quadratic in the form (x + p)² + q to find its vertex or solve the equation.
A statement showing that one expression is greater than, less than, or not equal to another.
A set of two or more equations with the same variables that are solved together.
Solving simultaneous equations by adding or subtracting equations to remove one variable.
Solving simultaneous equations by expressing one variable in terms of the other and substituting.
The value b²−4ac in the quadratic formula; determines the number of real solutions.
An ordered list of numbers or terms that follow a rule or pattern.
Each individual number or expression in a sequence.
A formula in terms of n that gives the value of any term in a sequence.
A sequence with a constant difference between consecutive terms, e.g. 3, 7, 11, 15…
A sequence where each term is multiplied by a constant ratio to get the next term.
A sequence where each term is the sum of the two preceding terms: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8…
A rule that assigns exactly one output to each input, written as f(x).
A function that reverses the effect of another function, written as f⁻¹(x).
Applying one function to the result of another, written as f(g(x)) or fg(x).
The set of all possible input values for a function.
The steepness of a line, calculated as rise ÷ run or (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁).
The point where a graph crosses the y-axis, where x = 0.
The equation of a straight line where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept.
Lines with the same gradient that never meet.
Lines that meet at 90°; their gradients multiply to give −1.
A curved U-shaped (or ∩-shaped) graph of a quadratic function, called a parabola.
The maximum or minimum point of a parabola where the curve changes direction.
The x-values where a graph crosses or touches the x-axis (where y = 0).
Shifting a graph horizontally or vertically using vector notation, e.g. f(x + a) or f(x) + a.
Flipping a graph in an axis: f(−x) reflects in the y-axis; −f(x) reflects in the x-axis.
A comparison of two or more quantities showing their relative sizes, written with a colon, e.g. 3:5.
Dividing all parts of a ratio by their highest common factor to give the simplest form.
Sharing a quantity into parts according to a given ratio by finding the value of one part first.
A relationship where two quantities increase or decrease at the same rate; y = kx.
A relationship where as one quantity increases the other decreases proportionally; y = k/x.
Finding the value of one unit first, then multiplying to find any other amount.
The ratio by which all lengths of a shape are multiplied when enlarging or reducing it.
Comparing value for money by calculating the cost per unit for each option.
The rate at which one currency can be converted into another.
The fixed multiplier in a proportion relationship, e.g. in y = kx, k = y/x.
How quickly one quantity changes relative to another, e.g. speed is the rate of change of distance.
The distance travelled per unit of time; Speed = Distance ÷ Time.
Mass per unit volume; Density = Mass ÷ Volume.
Force per unit area; Pressure = Force ÷ Area.
Interest calculated on both the original amount and any previously earned interest each period.
Interest calculated only on the original principal each period: I = PRT/100.
The decimal factor used to calculate a percentage increase or decrease in one step.
Adding a percentage of the original value: new value = original × (1 + r/100).
Subtracting a percentage of the original value: new value = original × (1 − r/100).
Finding the original value before a percentage change by dividing by the multiplier.
An angle that is greater than 0° and less than 90°.
An angle that is greater than 90° and less than 180°.
An angle that is greater than 180° and less than 360°.
Angles formed opposite each other when two lines cross; they are always equal.
Equal angles formed on opposite sides of a transversal cutting parallel lines ('Z-angles').
Angles on the same side of a transversal between parallel lines that add up to 180° ('C-angles').
Equal angles in matching positions when a transversal crosses parallel lines ('F-angles').
A direction measured clockwise from north, always written as a three-digit number, e.g. 045°.
An angle inside a polygon between two adjacent sides.
The angle formed outside a polygon between one side and the extension of the adjacent side.
A closed 2D shape with straight sides.
A polygon where all sides are equal in length and all interior angles are equal.
For any polygon with n sides: sum = (n − 2) × 180°.
A polygon with four sides; interior angles always sum to 360°.
The perimeter of a circle; C = πd or C = 2πr.
A part of the circumference of a circle.
A 'pie-slice' region of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc.
A straight line connecting two points on the circumference of a circle.
A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
A region of a circle bounded by a chord and the arc it cuts off.
The total length of the boundary of a 2D shape.
The amount of space enclosed within a 2D shape, measured in square units.
The total area of all the faces of a 3D solid.
The amount of 3D space enclosed within a solid, measured in cubic units.
A 3D solid with a uniform cross-section; volume = area of cross-section × length.
A prism with a circular cross-section; volume = πr²h.
A solid with a circular base tapering to a point; volume = ⅓πr²h.
A perfectly round 3D solid; volume = (4/3)πr³, surface area = 4πr².
A solid with a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at an apex; volume = ⅓ × base area × height.
A shape made up of two or more standard shapes joined together.
A transformation that moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction, described by a vector.
A transformation that flips a shape in a mirror line, producing a congruent image.
A transformation that turns a shape through an angle about a fixed centre point.
A transformation that changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre of enlargement.
Shapes that are identical in size and shape; one can be mapped onto the other by a rigid transformation.
Shapes that are the same shape but different sizes; all corresponding angles are equal and sides are in proportion.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, written as a column vector or using bold letters.
The fixed point from which an enlargement is made.
An enlargement where the image is on the opposite side of the centre and inverted.
A point that does not change position under a transformation.
In a right-angled triangle: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, always opposite the right angle.
In a right-angled triangle: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.
In a right-angled triangle: cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.
In a right-angled triangle: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.
A rule relating sides and angles in any triangle: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
A rule for any triangle: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
Area = ½ab sin C, used when two sides and the included angle are known.
Known exact values: sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2, and equivalents for cos and tan.
The angle measured upward (elevation) or downward (depression) from the horizontal.
A measure of how likely an event is to occur, expressed as a value between 0 and 1.
Probability calculated from equally likely outcomes: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
Probability estimated from trials: frequency of event ÷ total number of trials.
Events that cannot both occur at the same time; P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
Events where the outcome of one does not affect the other; P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
A diagram showing all possible outcomes of combined events as branches, with probabilities on each branch.
A diagram using overlapping circles to show the relationship between sets of outcomes.
The probability of an event given that another event has already occurred; P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B).
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.
The number of times an event is expected to occur: probability × number of trials.
The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when all data is arranged in order; for an even count, the mean of the two middle values.
The value that appears most frequently in a data set.
The difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set; a measure of spread.
The difference between the upper quartile (Q3) and the lower quartile (Q1); IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Values that divide an ordered dataset into four equal parts: Q1 (25%), Q2 (50%), Q3 (75%).
A data value that lies far outside the general pattern of the rest of the data.
A table showing how many times each value or group of values occurs in a dataset.
Data organised into class intervals when the range of values is large.
The mean calculated from grouped data using the midpoint of each class interval.
A chart using bars of equal width to show the frequency of each category or class interval.
A chart for continuous data where area of each bar represents frequency; bars can have different widths.
The value used on the y-axis of a histogram: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
A running total of frequencies; plotted as a curve to find medians and quartiles.
A diagram showing the minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum of a dataset.
A graph that plots pairs of values to show a possible relationship (correlation) between two variables.
The relationship between two variables; can be positive, negative, or none.
A straight line drawn through a scatter graph that best represents the trend in the data.
Using a line of best fit to estimate a value within the range of the data.
Using a line of best fit to estimate a value outside the range of the data; less reliable.
